# Discussion {#sec-discussion}

```{r}
#| label: p2b-disc-setup
#| include: false
loadNamespace("mlogit")   # so summary.mlogit dispatches (CLAUDE.md note)
p_rank   <- summary(model_2b_exploded_draw_final)$CoefTable["stall_x_wolverhampton", "Pr(>|z|)"]
roi_gain <- sprintf("%+.1f pp", 100 * roi_difference_2b_vs_2a$diff_point)
or_over_disc   <- scales::percent(value_bet_baselines_2b$over_round[1] - 1, accuracy = 1)
fav_tie_pct    <- scales::percent(backtest_favourite_win$n_tie_races /
                                  backtest_favourite_win$n_bets, accuracy = 0.1)
```

The exploded model predicts the top-3 finishing order with skill clearly
above chance, yet on neither ranking metric does it match the market. That is
the same pattern papers 1 and 2a found on the win objective — a model with
genuine signal that the starting price nonetheless out-scores — now repeated
on the ranking objective. The reading carries over unchanged: the market
price aggregates information the pre-race feature set does not contain. On
ranking accuracy (Q1), the market leads on both metrics — the ranking
objective does not close that gap. On win prediction (Q2), the ranking-fitted
model does better than paper 2a's win-fitted model, the first improvement in
the series that clears zero. Turned into bets, the model's place and each-way
strategies both lose.

The second question applies the ranking-fitted model to the win objective,
and here the result is new to the series. Trained on the finishing order
rather than on the winner alone, the model is a better winner-picker than
paper 2a's model: a paired race-level bootstrap puts the gain at
`r roi_gain`, with a 90% interval that lies above zero — the first
distinguishable improvement across the three papers. The improvement comes
from richer training data, not a different model. Depth-3 explosion gives
roughly three times as many choice problems from the same races, producing
sharper coefficient estimates for the same features. Wolverhampton is the
clean illustration: its draw term was too noisy to retain when the model was
fitted on wins alone ($p \approx 0.066$) but is estimated sharply under the
ranking objective ($p =$ `r sprintf("%.4f", p_rank)`), with the same sign and
a similar magnitude. The reading is the narrow one — the ranking objective
estimates the same draw effect paper 2a saw, sharply enough to retain it — not
a new effect uncovered. Both models still lose money; the
`r scales::percent(backtest_naive_2b_win$roi, accuracy = 0.1)` is better than
2a's `r scales::percent(backtest_naive_w_final$roi, accuracy = 0.1)`, but
neither beats the market.

Paper 3 will change the model class. A tree-based learner accommodates
non-linearities and feature interactions directly — among them a horse's
going affinity, which the conditional logit can express only through explicit
interaction terms — without the modeller specifying each one in advance.

Turned into bets, a realistic one-bet-per-race strategy is materially better
than backing every qualifier: place returns
`r scales::percent(backtest_single_place_2b$roi, accuracy = 0.1)` and each-way
`r scales::percent(backtest_single_eachway_2b$roi, accuracy = 0.1)`, against
`r scales::percent(backtest_place_2b$roi, accuracy = 0.1)` and
`r scales::percent(backtest_eachway_2b$roi, accuracy = 0.1)` for the multi-bet
rule — the paper's applied finding, and a place/each-way effect only (on the
win market single-bet gives no advantage:
`r scales::percent(backtest_single_win_2b$roi, accuracy = 0.1)` here,
`r scales::percent(backtest_single_win_2a$roi, accuracy = 0.1)` for paper 2a).
The losses are still dominated by the SP margin, not mis-selection: backing
every runner at SP loses
`r scales::percent(backtest_betall_win$roi, accuracy = 0.1)` and backing the
favourite `r scales::percent(backtest_favourite_win$roi, accuracy = 0.1)`[^fav-ties],
so the model's win selections sit between a zero-skill floor and a trivial
heuristic. But single-bet place at
`r scales::percent(backtest_single_place_2b$roi, accuracy = 0.1)` against a
~`r or_over_disc` SP over-round is roughly half the structural drag, and
against a lower-friction market such as a Betfair exchange (~5% commission)
that margin is far smaller — a direction worth testing, left to a future paper.

[^fav-ties]: Ties for favourite — the lowest decimal starting price shared by
two or more runners — occur in `r fav_tie_pct` of test races and are broken
here by taking the lower-numbered runner.
